## A · Precision conservation in tile-drained agricultural watersheds {#precision-conservation}

<p class="case-status"><span class="status-label">Completed · published</span> PhD research, University of Guelph, 2022–2026</p>

<dl class="case-study">
<div><dt>Research question</dt><dd>In a tile-drained agricultural watershed, which fields should receive which conservation practices so that nutrient losses fall, and how can that ranking reflect what local farmers and conservation staff consider feasible?</dd></div>
<div><dt>Why it matters</dt><dd>Nutrient losses from farmland contribute to algal blooms and degraded water quality in the Great Lakes. Subsurface tile drainage changes how water and nutrients leave a field, so a practice that works on one field may do little on another. Conservation budgets are limited, and programs that treat all fields alike spend much of that budget where it achieves least.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Study context</dt><dd>Tile-drained agricultural watersheds of the Laurentian Great Lakes Basin in Ontario. From 2024 to 2026 the work was supported by project funding from Environment and Climate Change Canada and involved collaboration with Environment and Climate Change Canada, Iowa State University and academic partners.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Methods and data</dt><dd>Two structured literature reviews; GIS and terrain analysis, including the Agricultural Conservation Planning Framework (ACPF), to map where practices are physically suitable; machine learning to predict field-level conservation need and to map the uncertainty of those predictions; distributed, process-based watershed modelling to evaluate practices; and a prioritisation method whose weights stakeholders can adjust.</dd></div>
<div><dt>My role</dt><dd>I led the research as a doctoral candidate and am first author of all four papers. I carried out the reviews, spatial analysis and modelling and wrote the manuscripts, working with my advisory committee and co-authors from the University of Guelph and partner agencies.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Published findings</dt><dd><ul><li>Existing spatial decision-support tools for precision conservation seldom combine environmental modelling with economic trade-offs and stakeholder knowledge. The 2023 review proposes a framework that links the three.</li><li>The performance of conservation practices in tile-drained Great Lakes watersheds varies by site, which supports combining practices across field and watershed scales rather than relying on any single practice (2025 review).</li><li>Machine learning can predict field-level conservation need and map prediction uncertainty, giving planners a basis for choosing intervention sites (2026).</li><li>Field-specific conservation options can be ranked by combining landscape suitability, feasibility and priorities that stakeholders adjust to local needs (2026).</li></ul><p class="case-note">These statements summarise the published papers. They do not report results beyond them.</p></dd></div>
<div><dt>Relevance</dt><dd>The work gives conservation authorities and agricultural agencies a way to direct cost-share funding to the fields where it is likely to do most, and to explain those choices to producers. It is directly relevant to nutrient-reduction commitments for Lake Erie and to stewardship programs across southern Ontario.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Publications</dt><dd><ul class="case-pubs"><li>Bodrud-Doza, M., et al. (2026). Operationalizing precision conservation: Aligning best management practice prioritization with local needs in agricultural watersheds. <em>International Soil and Water Conservation Research</em>. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.iswcr.2026.100688">doi:10.1016/j.iswcr.2026.100688</a></li><li>Bodrud-Doza, M., et al. (2026). Advancing precision conservation through machine learning for field-level prioritization of agricultural best management practices. <em>International Soil and Water Conservation Research</em>. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.iswcr.2026.100668">doi:10.1016/j.iswcr.2026.100668</a></li><li>Bodrud-Doza, M., et al. (2025). Evaluating best management practices for nutrient load reductions in tile-drained watersheds of the Laurentian Great Lakes Basin: A literature review. <em>Science of The Total Environment</em>, 965, 178657. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2025.178657">doi:10.1016/j.scitotenv.2025.178657</a></li><li>Bodrud-Doza, M., et al. (2023). Towards implementing precision conservation practices in agricultural watersheds: A review of the use and prospects of Spatial Decision Support Tools and Systems. <em>Science of the Total Environment</em>, 905, 167118. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2023.167118">doi:10.1016/j.scitotenv.2023.167118</a></li></ul><p>Plain-language accounts: <a href="https://theconversation.com/tackling-lake-eries-algal-blooms-requires-targeted-conservation-strategies-293913">The Conversation (2026)</a> and a <a href="https://www.uoguelph.ca/csahs/news/2026/07/following-flow-exploring-geography-cleaner-water">University of Guelph research story (2026)</a>. Full author lists are in the <a href="publications.qmd#publication-record">publication record</a>.</p></dd></div>
<div><dt>What comes next</dt><dd>Testing whether the approach transfers to watersheds with different drainage and data conditions, and adding costs and wider ecosystem benefits to the ranking. A proposal to the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Agribusiness (OMAFA) that would do this in the Lake Erie Basin is <a href="collaboration.qmd#omafa-precision-conservation-proposal">under review</a>; funding is not confirmed.</dd></div>
</dl>

## B · Healthy Lake Huron: watershed monitoring, modelling and conservation decision support {#healthy-lake-huron}

<p class="case-status"><span class="status-label active">Active · Mitacs Accelerate</span> Postdoctoral project, University of Guelph, September 2026–present</p>

<dl class="case-study">
<div><dt>Research question</dt><dd>How can long-term tributary monitoring and high-resolution watershed modelling be combined to explain what drives nutrient and sediment losses from small agricultural watersheds, and to give partners practical indicators for deciding where conservation investment should go?</dd></div>
<div><dt>Why it matters</dt><dd>Agricultural tributaries along the southeast shore of Lake Huron carry nutrients and sediment that affect nearshore water quality and beaches. Conservation authorities have monitored these streams and supported beneficial management practices (BMPs) for many years. Water-quality measurements alone respond slowly and vary strongly from year to year, which makes it hard to tell which actions are working and where to act next.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Partners and roles</dt><dd>The project connects University of Guelph research with <a href="https://healthylakehuron.ca/">Healthy Lake Huron partners</a>. <a href="https://www.abca.ca/">Ausable Bayfield Conservation Authority (ABCA)</a> is the formal Mitacs partner. ABCA, Maitland Valley Conservation Authority and the wider Healthy Lake Huron partnership contribute watershed data and expertise.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Methods and data</dt><dd>Long-term stream-flow, water-quality and land-management records held by partners; IMWEBs (Integrated Modelling for Watershed Evaluation of BMPs), a process-based watershed model developed at the University of Guelph; conservation and climate scenarios; and indicators that track both water-quality outcomes and the condition and management of the landscape.</dd></div>
<div><dt>My role</dt><dd>I am the postdoctoral scholar on the project and carry out the data integration, modelling and indicator development, working with my faculty supervisor and partner staff. I held a data-analyst position at ABCA in summer 2024, analysing long-term water-quality data from a Lake Huron tributary.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Current progress</dt><dd>The project began in September 2026 and is in its first phase. There are no project findings to report yet.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Workplan</dt><dd><ol class="project-sequence"><li>Monitoring &amp; Data</li><li>Modelling &amp; Scenarios</li><li>Indicators</li><li>Decisions</li></ol><p>The work moves from compiling and quality-checking partner datasets, to setting up and testing the watershed model, to comparing conservation and climate scenarios, to developing indicators and decision-support products with partners.</p></dd></div>
<div><dt>Planned deliverables</dt><dd>Conservation-priority maps, indicator scorecards and monitoring recommendations, together with journal articles. These are intended outputs. None has been delivered yet.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Relevance</dt><dd>The results are meant to help conservation authorities direct stewardship funding, refine monitoring, and report progress to producers, municipalities and governments in terms that can be checked.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Links</dt><dd><a href="https://healthylakehuron.ca/">Healthy Lake Huron</a> · <a href="collaboration.qmd#current-applied-collaboration">Partnership context</a> · <a href="research.qmd#current-and-developing-projects">Status of all current work</a></dd></div>
</dl>

## C · Future research: environmental intelligence and resilient agricultural landscapes {#environmental-intelligence}

<p class="case-status"><span class="status-label">Developing · research plan</span> No results are reported in this section</p>

<dl class="case-study">
<div><dt>Research questions</dt><dd><ul><li>Can satellite time series detect where and when cover, drainage and conservation practices change across whole agricultural regions, at a level of detail that field-scale planning can use?</li><li>How should observation-driven machine learning and process-based models be combined, so that predictions are both timely and physically credible?</li><li>How should conservation priorities be revised as monitoring shows what worked, and as climate and markets shift?</li><li>Which early signals show that an agricultural landscape or food system is losing its capacity to absorb shocks?</li></ul></dd></div>
<div><dt>Why it matters</dt><dd>Watershed plans are usually made once, from data that are already several years old. Monitoring is costly and sparse, and conditions change faster than plans are revised. Observation that is wider and more frequent, linked to models and to decision processes, would let agencies and producers adjust sooner and justify their choices better.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Approach</dt><dd>Combine three things I already work with (long-term monitoring records, process-based watershed models and machine learning) with satellite observation and GeoAI, and build the results into the Observe → Understand → Plan → Decide &amp; Learn cycle described on the <a href="research.qmd#four-connected-research-areas">Research page</a>.</dd></div>
<div><dt>What exists now</dt><dd>Published spatial-analysis and machine-learning research; professional training in remote sensing and Google Earth Engine; a co-authored <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fclim.2022.944736">review of disaster risk reduction and anticipatory action in Bangladesh</a> (2022); professional experience in climate adaptation; and the active Healthy Lake Huron project, which will supply a first test bed for indicators.</dd></div>
<div><dt>What does not exist yet</dt><dd>I have no publications in Earth observation or GeoAI and no funded project on food-system resilience. My application to the Canada Postdoctoral Research Award program for the food-system direction is submitted; no award is confirmed.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Relevance</dt><dd>The aim is conservation and adaptation planning that keeps pace with change: for water quality in the Great Lakes region, and for agricultural resilience in climate-exposed settings such as Bangladesh.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Opportunities</dt><dd>Graduate projects in satellite-based monitoring of conservation practices, model–data integration and indicator design; partnerships with conservation authorities and agricultural agencies; and comparative Canada–Bangladesh research. See the <a href="research.qmd#five-year-program">five-year plan</a> and <a href="collaboration.qmd">collaboration interests</a>.</dd></div>
</dl>
